reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / ESE-ENSAT Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Adrenal Incidentalomas
clinicalPearls: A benign, hormonally inactive adrenal tumour composed of mature adipose tissue admixed with haematopoietic (myeloid) elements
Diagnosis can often be made confidently on imaging by identifying macroscopic (bulk) fat within the lesion on CT or MRI
Most are small and asymptomatic and found incidentally, while large lesions may cause flank or abdominal pain from mass effect
Large myelolipomas carry a risk of spontaneous retroperitoneal haemorrhage, which increases as the tumour enlarges
They are generally non-functioning, although they occasionally coexist with endocrine disorders
Small, asymptomatic, characteristic lesions are managed with surveillance, whereas large, symptomatic or bleeding lesions may warrant surgical removal
The presence of macroscopic fat helps separate it from a lipid-rich adenoma, which contains only microscopic intracytoplasmic lipid, and from malignant tumours
reference.pathophysiology: Adrenal myelolipoma consists of mature fat mixed with haematopoietic tissue resembling bone marrow, arising from metaplasia of adrenocortical stromal cells, possibly under hormonal or stress-related stimuli. The lesion is benign and typically non-secreting. As it enlarges, its friable, vascular composition and high fat content predispose to spontaneous haemorrhage, which is the principal complication of large tumours.
additionalInvestigations: CT demonstrating macroscopic fat with markedly negative attenuation within the mass
MRI with fat-suppression sequences to confirm bulk fat
Hormonal screening with dexamethasone suppression, metanephrines and aldosterone-to-renin ratio as part of the incidentaloma workup
Assessment for haemorrhage if acute pain develops
Surgical referral for large or symptomatic lesions
redFlags: Acute severe flank or abdominal pain or haemodynamic instability suggesting haemorrhage
Large size with mass effect on adjacent structures
Atypical imaging with soft-tissue components raising concern for malignancy
reference.prognosis: Excellent; myelolipomas are benign and do not metastasise, and the outlook is determined mainly by size-related complications such as haemorrhage, which resolve well after treatment.
pitfalls: Mistaking a fat-containing myelolipoma for a malignant retroperitoneal fatty tumour
Underestimating the haemorrhage risk of a very large lesion
Omitting hormonal screening simply because myelolipomas are usually non-functioning
Performing unnecessary surgery for a small, characteristic, asymptomatic lesion
references: ESE-ENSAT Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Adrenal Incidentalomas
management: Confirm the benign diagnosis by demonstrating macroscopic bulk fat on CT or fat-suppression MRI
Screen biochemically as for any incidentaloma with dexamethasone suppression, metanephrines and aldosterone-to-renin ratio to confirm the lesion is non-functioning
Refer for surgical resection by adrenalectomy of large or symptomatic lesions given the heightened risk of spontaneous retroperitoneal haemorrhage
Monitor size on interval imaging where a large lesion is observed rather than resected
Resuscitate with fluid and blood replacement and stabilise urgently if acute retroperitoneal haemorrhage develops
Advise avoidance of flank trauma and prompt review for new or worsening flank pain
